OK guys, here is the problem explained more thoroughly.

Let's take one variable commonly used in programming .. line numbers
The Blue Ram Basic is going to get the answer for that calculation at the address of %(27789) which is %(6C8D) Hex. [ Written %(!6C8D) in BRB].When the basic is looking there, it interprets the number ferom that location. Viper may have it located somewhere else, so it can't find it. There are 85 different variables ranging fron 1 letter storage variables to the Primary Z80 Stack. They are located in the space between %(27680) (%(!6C20)) and %(28671) (%(!6FFF)). The open program areas are between %(24576) and %(27679) (%(!6000) & %(!6C1F)). This is inside the first 4K with the 85 above. The rest of the 16K starts at %(28672) and goes to %(-24449). (%(!7000) to %%(!A07F)) and %(!E07F) for 32k. If Viper or the others is looking elsewhere for the variable list that was saved with the program, wallah .. crash!!!
Ken

3556:
PRINT SZ will tell you how much memory you have available for program area (line numbered program). Blue Ram Basic 1.1 has the area from %(24576) to %(27679) and any expanded area above &(28672). You can use this area for storage and machine language. In a 16K expansion, this area is %(28672)  / %(7000) hex to %(-24449) / %(A07F) Hex. The 32K expansion goes to %(-8065) / %(E07F) hex. To use the hex numbers in Blue Ram 1.1 put an exclaimation point before the number, I.E. %(!7000).
The gap in the middle is where the variables are stored. From %(27680) / %(!6C20) to %(28671) / %(!6FFF).
If someone is creative in their programming, the can change the pionters located at !6C82,
!6C8D, !6C9C, !6FFC and !6FFE (see Blue Ram Detailed Memory Allocation chart under Perkins Engineering section of Bally Alley) during the operation of the program to utilize both the lower and the upper sections for numbered line programming.

I am not familiar with how ViperSoft addresses it's memory.

I hope this helps and doesn't confuse you too much.
Ken

3585:
As previously posted, Mike Peace sent me his collection of the
WaveMakers master tapes for archiving a few months ago.  So, when I've
had spare time, I've recorded, processed, and tested them.  And there
is a lot there.  Excluding extra RAM programs, which weren't included
in these tapes, I believe we now have some version of every known
WaveMakers program, and all versions of most of them.

I received 20 tapes.  These included master tapes for WaveMakers tapes
1-18, a mostly empty tape with no programs and a bit of music, and the
Game Selector, which collects several previously released programs
with a menu.  The list on Bally Alley
(http://www.ballyalley.com/misc_docs/Wavemakers_Tape_Listing.pdf) says
tapes 19 and 20 were also released, with programs like Outpost 19,
Tomb Pirates, and QB23.  These were not in the tapes I received, and
looking through references in the newsletters I couldn't tell that
they were ever officially released (except Outpost 19 in extended RAM
format).  Does anyone know more about this?  In any case, these had
previously been archived, probably from Mike White.

The content of the tapes was mostly as expected.  Tapes 1-10 had
multiple main programs in both 2000 and 300 baud formats, along with
assorted freebee programs, not necessarily repeated in both formats.
A 300 baud program would generally just be present once on the tape,
while 2000 baud programs were repeated on each side.  The code for a
300 baud program might be a bit different, but they seemed to play the
same.  Tape 11, Whiz Quiz, didn't have any repeats due to its length,
just a 2000 baud side and a 300 baud side.  In this case, the 300 baud
program actually has different questions!  The remaining tapes had
only 2000 baud programs, and usually only the main programs.  I was
somewhat surprised at the extra programs present on tapes 17 and 18.
These had many repeats.  Tape 17 (L.T.) included Memory Lane,
Wack-A-Mole, and Music Keyboard.  Tape 18 (Gate Escape) included
Wack-A-Mole and Music Keyboard.  I wonder if the tapes were actually
released with this format.  One program I didn't know existed was an
advertisement for Castle Of Horror on the Obstacle Course Tournament
tape.  I also found three spoken introductions to Invasion Force (a
freebee) and a spoken introduction to The Gate Escape.  These were
very brief, just identifying the program.  I wonder why this technique
was only used a few times.

I did encounter a few problems in the archiving.  I was unable to get
all of the loads of the 2000 baud version of Whiz Quiz to process
correctly.  This is already on-line, from Mike White.  In
investigating this, I realized that Mike White had removed repeated
portions from his version.  So, I decided to just reformat his into
the original form and call it good.  I also couldn't get Character
Analysis completely working, but again, we already have a good version
of this from Mike White.  There were also problems with the Game
Selector.  Side 1 is complete on the tape, but I could never get the
fifth of ten loads to process correctly.  This should be Space Chase.
 For now, I've made a version missing this load, which works fine as
long as you don't want to play Space Chase.  I haven't heard anything
recently about a Ballybin update, but perhaps this could help get this
one completely archived.  Oddly, side 2 of the Game Selector was
actually incomplete on the tape.  It had only six loads, which all
processed correctly.  So, in the present version, the menu choices 3,
4, 6, and 9 won't work.  In both sides, the order of programs on the
tape and on the menu is different.

There are also a few problems with the 300 baud programs.  Whiz Quiz
has a few errors which I saw very consistently, like stray question
marks in questions.  In no case does this make the program crash or
work incorrectly, so I've decided to just upload it as is.  This is
the master tape, so it's even possible these errors were present on
the commercially released tapes.  I also saw very consistent errors in
the 300 baud version of Flying Ace.  I find it less likely that these
were present originally because the program won't work.  The code is
different than the 2000 baud version, but I made my best guess at
repairs and the program still crashed.  Does anyone want to look at
this?  On the same tape, the 300 baud version of WaveMakers Fortune
Teller didn't quite work as expected.  There was a question mark near
the end, and of greater concern, the program would only print out two
fortunes before stopping.  I'm not sure if I should upload this or not.

I should make a few notes about naming.  I named these programs
without regard for the programs currently on-line, the idea being that
anything extra on-line should become alternate version of the programs
on the master tapes.  When I could tell a difference between programs,
or if I wanted to note what tape a freebee came from, I noted this in
the name.  If they seemed the same, I used v1, v2, etc.  I've scanned
these for exact binary duplicates, and found several, but there are
still programs which seem to play the same but aren't exactly the same
file.  In some cases, I decided the best name was slightly different
than the one on Mike White's list.  For example, the title screen of
the 1982 version of Flying Ace actually says Flying Ace '82', so
that's what I called it.

While the archiving is basically complete, the organization probably
isn't.  In particular, I'd like to know how Adam want to get these
organized.  I'd like to take this opportunity to reorganize the
WaveMakers section with the best names for everything.  A few programs
now on-line are exact duplicates of the ones I archived, so one
version can be deleted.  In other cases, the ones on-line can become
alternate versions.  I can test these to see if I notice any
differences.  Hopefully we can note somewhere where the programs came
from (master tapes, Mike White, etc.).  I don't know if Adam wants to
make detailed text files for these as he did for the last big set of
programs.

This also brings up the question of the back-log of uploads.  Adam, is
there content almost ready to go on-line from the work you did around
Christmas, or did you mainly just work on the game catalog?  I'm
trying to make sure nothing gets forgotten as so many things are in
various states of preparation.

baud programs, since I've been archiving many
recently.  I just announced some WaveMakers programs
coming up.

AstroBASIC doesn't come up to a menu like most carts;
it goes straight to a white screen with a very simple
BASIC prompt.  The original version (without the
built-in audio interface) said "BALLY BASIC," but they
took this out in the update to save a bit of memory. 
The red LED is to indicate that audio is being
received.  When inputting audio data, it should be
bright red.  During normal operation it will stay off.

Hopefully Lance's cleaning tips will help.  But if you
can't get it working, the carts are readily available
on eBay.

Paul

3633:
Well, I'd probably better answer Adam's questions about archiving
before I forget how I did it.  :-)

I suppose it actually all started when Adam first interviewed Mike
Peace for Bally Alley, and Mike released his programs to the public
domain and mentioned still having the master tapes.  Over the next few
years various programs were archived, including many games by
WaveMakers.  Then I got involved with sorting through previously
recorded tapes and archiving new tapes as well.  At this point, we had
a pretty good WaveMakers collection, but there were still a lot of
gaps, with no obvious way to get the missing tapes.

Then in March 2006, Adam took the initiative of e-mailing Mike again
to point out some recently uploaded material and ask about borrowing
the master tapes for archiving, and suggested that I talk to  Mike
about making arrangements.  There was some difficulty with Mike not
getting our e-mails, but with the help of contact information on his
music site I eventually got a dialog going and he agreed to loan me
the tapes.

So, in July 2006 I got a box of 20 cassettes, mostly labeled by tape
number.  By this point I was well acquainted with the ways of
Astrocade tape archiving, but it was still a lot to deal with.  And
even though we already had some programs, I decided to go ahead and
archive everything since some programs have multiple versions.

So, over the next few months I worked a bit at a time on archiving all
the tapes.  First, I would record a tape onto my computer as a .wav
file.  Then, by listening and looking at the waveform, I could tell a
bit about the organization, such as what parts were 2000 baud and 300
baud.  The 2000 baud sections I processed with Ballybin and then
tested on my Astrocade.  The 300 baud sections I loaded directly from
the raw data.  Sometimes, something didn't quite work and I'd make
another recording and try again.

For the most part, this worked well, but the biggest frustrations were
of course when I couldn't get something to work correctly.  We still
don't have a working 300 baud version of Flying Ace, for instance, and
while the 300 and 2000 baud versions of programs tend to play the
same, they aren't always identical.  In particular, the BASIC code for
the 300 baud Flying Ace isn't the same.  I also had trouble with the
programs with huge numbers of loads--Whiz Quiz and Character Analysis.
 I started to process and test the 2000 baud version of Whiz Quiz one
load at a time, but was almost glad to realize that some just didn't
work, and decided that the data we'd previously gotten from Mike White
would have to suffice.  I did test every question from Mike White's
version to ensure it had been archived correctly, and rearranged the
data into its original format.  This got somewhat annoying after
awhile, but did undoubtedly increase my knowledge of 1970's TV shows.  :-)

It was already largely known what WaveMakers programs had been made.
I was hoping I might find some previously unknown prototype game or
something, but that didn't happen.  Really the only unexpected program
was a promotion for Castle Of Horror found on the Obstacle Course
Tournament tape.  I also hadn't realized that the 300 baud version of
Whiz Quiz had different questions than the 2000 baud version.
Normally there isn't much reason to play the 300 baud version of
program available in 2000 baud format (though it's good to archive for
completeness), but this is an exception.  This process also answered
my questions about the different versions of Lookout For The Bull!  It
turns out that Lookout For The Bull! II is essentially the same game,
but with simpler graphics and presumably more difficult.  I actually
couldn't tell much difference, but maybe you need to advance to the
later levels.

I've sent Mike Peace a few notes to keep track of my progress, but
that's really been our only interaction.  I have asked about any
instructions and such he might have, so maybe there will be more
archiving to come.  Already we have quite a good WaveMakers collection
ready to go on-line.  I'm always glad to see tape archiving get to the
point where the programs for a company are thoroughly archived, rather
than just a few scattered games being saved.  This happened previously
with Esoterica, and I hope it will happen again in the future.  (Any
more L&M games out there?)

While archiving these programs was definitely a lot of work, I'm glad
I did it.  Not only have I helped preserve a part of videogame
history, I got to play some cool games along the way.  As simple as it
is, I got lots of practice on Obstacle Course Tournament, in addition
to getting more experience with the games that had already been
archived.  I hope that once everything's on-line, everyone tries out
some programs.  What's your favorite WaveMakers game?  I say of the
newly archived ones, Obstacle Course Tournament, and overall, Tomb
Pirates.

Paul

You can transfer files from the PC to the Astrocade and play games, but these are not ROM files (i.e. these are not cartridges).  These are games that were originally released on casette tape and were written in BASIC (or machine language) that are loaded via the BASIC cartridge as WAV files.

There is no device for the Astrocade that lets you load ROM files into a RAM cartidge.  If you want to play ROM files, then you'll have to get a rather rare Astrocade multicart, or you make make your own cartridges by burning the ROM files to an EPROM.

This probably leaves you with more questions than it answers, but I can't fully answer your question without more knowledge of what you are asking about.

We're pretty friendly around here and we welcome newbie questions of any sort.  The most frequently asked question is how to repair a dead Astrocade; it is a nice change to get a question about how to play games on the actual hardware!

This is the original BASIC, referred to as Bally BASIC.  The newer version is known as AstroBASIC.  If you have the BASIC interface that plugs into the joystick port and the lightpen port, then you can load some of the 300 BAUD programs.  These programs are here:

At last count there were about four-hundred programs that you could load into the Astrocade.  To get you started, I recommend trying some of the games by WaveMakers.

2) Most of the time you just need to type: :INPUT;RUN

3641:
I think what you are asking is how the CPU timing aligns with the video
timing.  In the 2600, for instance, most CPU events line up to the pixel so
that when you make realtime changes to registers, you (usually) get nice
clean results.  Not the case with most other systems (if you can do these
things at all).

I know on the Bally there is a VBI-like function you can call to change
color registers between scanlines but this was very rarely used.  This is a
shame since it has a very rich 256 color palette.  The Bally has half the
vertical resolution of the 2600 (although not all 2600 games fully utilize
its max resolution) but you'd think it could do the same kind of gradients
and palette "zones" you see on the VCS and Atari 8-bit.

I don't know if the system allows you to do anything meaningful in

The Bally Astrocade FAQ (http://www.ballyalley.com/faqs/bally-astrocade_faq.txt) has an entire section about heatsinks.

Many people that have working Astrocades (and want to keep them that way) will remove the metal shielding from the inside of their Astrocade, attach large rubber feet to the bottom of the Astrocade, and will ALWAYS keep their Astrocade off of carpet.  Some people have put heatsinks on the hot chips and other have put fans on their installed heat sinks.

If nothing else, then I would AT LEAST advise you to remove the shielding-- it makes the inside of the Astrocade HOT.  However, in order to do this you'll need a high-temp soldering gun and some desoldering wick, as the shielding is soldered in place rather well.  You'll have little luck trying to remove the solder from the metal shielding with a low-temp iron, as the metal shielding acts as a heatsink (wouldn't you know it!).  Personally, when I use my Astrocade often, I don't even put the plastic cover back on while I'm using it.

If anyone has some other suggestions, than I'd like to hear them.
